sources.title: NGSS 4-PS4-2: Develop a model to describe that light reflecting from objects and entering the eye allows objects to be seen
OpenStax University Physics Volume 3, 1.2 The Law of Reflection

note.text: The sun gives off its own light. Things that give off light, like the sun or a lamp, are light sources.
Light spreads out from the sun in every direction.

steps.title: Apple
steps.instruction: Trace the apple and its stem.

note.text: An apple makes no light of its own. We can only see it when light shines on it.
note.remember: Most things don't make their own light.

steps.title: Eye
steps.instruction: Trace the eye and its colored iris.

note.text: Your eye takes in light. Inside, it turns the light into signals for your brain.

steps.title: Light's path
steps.instruction: Draw the light from the sun to the apple, then from the apple to the eye.

note.text: Light bounces, or reflects, off the apple. Some of it enters your eye, and that's how you see the apple.
note.remember: We see light that reflects into our eyes.

steps.title: How you see
steps.why: Light from a source hits the apple, reflects off it, and travels into your eye.
steps.hint: Where does the light come from?

steps.title: Explain
steps.question: In a room with no light at all, can you see the apple?

options.text: No, because no light can reflect off it into your eyes
options.feedback: Right. Seeing needs light to bounce off the apple and enter your eyes. With no light, there's nothing to see.

options.text: Yes, if you look hard enough
options.feedback: Looking harder doesn't help: you can only see light that enters your eyes.
Apples don't make their own light. They can only be seen by light reflecting off them.

options.text: Only if it's a red apple
options.feedback: Color doesn't matter. Without light to reflect, you can't see any apple.

steps.title: Explain
steps.question: Why can everyone in a classroom see the same poster, wherever they sit?

options.text: Its rough surface reflects light in every direction
options.feedback: Yes. Rough surfaces like paper scatter light every way, so some reaches every eye in the room.

options.text: The poster makes its own light
options.feedback: Posters don't make light. They reflect light in every direction.
That's how a mirror reflects. Rough paper scatters light in every direction.
Size isn't the reason. Its rough surface reflects light every way, into every eye.
